title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
author: Robert T. Kiyosaki
tagline: What the rich teach their kids about money that the poor and middle class do not.
overview: Kiyosaki contrasts the lessons of his educated but struggling 'poor dad' with those of his friend's entrepreneurial 'rich dad'. The book's core message is financial literacy: understand assets versus liabilities, build your own asset column and make money work for you.

chapters.title: Rich Dad, Poor Dad
chapters.summary: Kiyosaki grew up with two father figures holding opposite views of money. His poor dad valued safe jobs and saw money as scarce; his rich dad saw money as a tool and taught him to ask 'How can I afford it?' instead of saying 'I can't afford it'. That shift in thinking frames the book.
keyIdeas: Financial education isn't taught in school.
chapters.tryThis: Next time you think 'I can't afford it', ask 'How could I afford it?'

quiz.question: What question did rich dad encourage?
quiz.explanation: It opens the mind to solutions.

chapters.title: Lesson 1: The Rich Don't Work for Money
chapters.summary: Working as a boy for almost nothing, Kiyosaki learned that fear and desire trap most people in a cycle of working for pay. Rich dad taught him to use his mind to spot opportunities and to make money work for him rather than becoming a lifelong worker for money.
keyIdeas: Fear and greed drive the rat race.
chapters.tryThis: List one way your money could earn money for you.

quiz.question: What keeps people in the rat race per Kiyosaki?
quiz.explanation: Emotions drive people to keep working for pay.

chapters.title: Lesson 2: Why Teach Financial Literacy?
chapters.summary: What matters isn't how much you earn but how much you keep. Kiyosaki defines an asset as something that puts money in your pocket and a liability as something that takes money out. The rich acquire assets; the poor and middle class acquire liabilities they believe are assets.
keyIdeas: Assets put money in your pocket.
It's what you keep that counts.
chapters.tryThis: Sort what you own into assets and liabilities by Kiyosaki's definition.

quiz.question: How does Kiyosaki define an asset?
options: Something that puts money in your pocket
quiz.explanation: Cash flow in, not perceived value.

chapters.title: Lesson 3: Mind Your Own Business
chapters.summary: Your profession is not your business; your business is your asset column. Keep your day job, but steadily build assets — businesses, stocks, bonds, real estate, royalties — and avoid buying luxuries until your assets can pay for them.
keyIdeas: Your business is your asset column.
chapters.tryThis: Choose one asset type to learn about this month.

quiz.question: What does 'mind your own business' mean here?
options: Focus on building your asset column
quiz.explanation: Your assets are your real business.

chapters.title: Lesson 4: The History of Taxes and the Power of Corporations
chapters.summary: Kiyosaki argues that taxes weigh hardest on employees, while the financially educated use legal structures such as corporations to earn, spend and then pay tax. He stresses knowing the rules — accounting, investing, markets and law — to protect your wealth legally.
keyIdeas: Corporations change the order of spending and taxes.
Learn accounting, investing, markets and law.
chapters.tryThis: Learn how your own income is taxed and one legal way to plan around it.

quiz.question: Which is part of Kiyosaki's 'financial IQ'?
quiz.explanation: He lists accounting, investing, markets and law.

chapters.title: Lesson 5: The Rich Invent Money
chapters.summary: Financial intelligence lets people create opportunities others miss. Kiyosaki encourages being willing to take calculated risks, learning continuously and seeing deals with creativity, rather than waiting for a perfect, risk-free moment.
chapters.tryThis: Study one deal or investment idea in detail this week.

quiz.question: What lets the rich 'invent money'?
quiz.explanation: Knowledge lets them spot and create opportunities.

chapters.title: Lesson 6: Work to Learn — Don't Work for Money
chapters.summary: Choose jobs for the skills they teach, not just the pay. Kiyosaki highlights sales and communication, management and broad business skills, arguing that many talented people stay poor because they know a lot about one thing but little about selling and systems.
keyIdeas: Work for skills, not just salary.
chapters.tryThis: Pick one skill — like sales — to deliberately improve this year.

quiz.question: Which skills does Kiyosaki stress learning?

chapters.title: Overcoming Obstacles
chapters.summary: Kiyosaki names five obstacles that stop people from building wealth even with knowledge: fear, cynicism, laziness, bad habits and arrogance. Each can be overcome — for example, by paying yourself first and asking 'what am I missing?'
keyIdeas: Fear, cynicism, laziness, habits and arrogance block wealth.
chapters.tryThis: Set up an automatic transfer to savings or investing on payday.

chapters.title: Getting Started
chapters.summary: Kiyosaki offers steps to awaken financial genius: find a strong reason, make daily choices, pick friends carefully, master a formula then learn new ones, pay yourself first, pay advisers well, give to receive, and use assets to buy luxuries.
keyIdeas: Choose how you spend time and money.
chapters.tryThis: Write your 'why' for building wealth in one paragraph.

quiz.question: What does Kiyosaki say to start with?

chapters.title: Still Want More? Here Are Some To Do's
chapters.summary: The closing chapter lists practical actions: stop doing what isn't working, look for new ideas, find people who've done what you want, take classes, make many offers, and get into the market rather than only reading about it.
keyIdeas: Learn from people who've done it.
chapters.tryThis: Talk to one person who already has the financial result you want.

quiz.question: What's a recurring theme of the to-do list?
options: Take action and learn from doers
